newsitem.title: USA: Alabama jury recommends death in mail-bomb case.
newsitem.headline: Alabama jury recommends death in mail-bomb case.

text.p: An Alabama jury on Tuesday recommended the death penalty for a 61-year-old man convicted in the 1989 mail-bomb murder of a federal appellate court judge.

The Jefferson County Circuit Court panel of nine women and three men found Walter Leroy Moody guilty on two counts of capital murder and one count of first degree assault early on their second day of deliberations.
By a vote of 11 to 1, the same jury later recommended that Moody be put to death in the state's electric chair. State Circuit Judge William Rhea did not set a sentencing date.

Moody was convicted on state charges in the murder of U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Vance, who died at his Mountain Brook home seven years ago while opening a package that contained a bomb. The judge's wife, Helen Vance, was injured in the blast.

Since 1991, the defendant has been serving a federal sentence of life without parole for killing Vance and Robert Robinson, a lawyer from Savannah, Georgia, who also died in a mail-bombing in December 1989.

Authorities say Moody planted four bombs in total, but two of the devices were discovered before they detonated. His bombing campaign was said to have been motivated by his frustration over his failure to get a 1972 federal conviction for possessing a pipe bomb overturned.

"Moody is a conniver. He has always been someone who has tried to manipulate the system. And I hope he gets manipulated in Yellow Mama's lap," prosecutor Bob Morrow said, using the macabre prison slang for Alabama's electric chair.

While representing himself at the trial, Moody spent days berating Rhea and prosecution witnesses as Morrow tried to link him to the murder. But by the end of the proceedings he had retreated into silence and ignored his chance to make a closing statement to the jury.

His ex-wife Susan Moody Samford testified that she had bought the cardboard baxes, flashlight batteries and bulbs, aluminum pie plates, and mailing packets and labels used to package the bomb that killed Vance. His girlfriend, Karlene Shiver, told jurors Moody had talked about how a bombing could be the perfect crime.

Prosecutors also presented Moody's own mutterings to himself about his hatred for courts and judges. The remarks, recorded by FBI microphones hidden in his home in 1990, included a muttered reference to two fatal bombings.

"The evidence was overwhelming," juror Glen Apperson of Birmingham later said. "Between the evidence of the girlfriend, ex-wife and the government's corroborating evidence, it was totally convincing."
